channel.title: Practical Rewards Blog
channel.description: Straight answers about credit cards, points, cash back, and the fine print.

item.title: Does a Statement Credit Cover Your Minimum Payment?
item.description: A $50 rewards credit can leave a $40 minimum payment due. See the hypothetical math, the limited exception, and what to check before paying.

item.title: Before You Cancel a Companion Fare Booking, Check the Code
item.description: Canceling a companion-fare ticket can forfeit an expired code. Check the original expiration and fare rules before changing your plans.

item.title: Want a Credit Card Recommendation? Start With This Short Note
item.description: Better card advice starts with your payment habits, everyday spending, current cards, travel plans, and tolerance for tracking perks. Rough totals are enough.

item.title: Should You Add Points to a Marriott Free Night Award?
item.description: Add points only when the better stay earns its keep. Compare certificate-only options, extra points, cash costs, and another use before expiration.

item.title: The $6,000 Question Before You Chase a Companion Fare
item.description: Before moving spending for a companion fare, compare the rewards you give up, the points you earn, and whether you will actually use the discount.

item.title: Marriott Boundless Credit Limit: What You Can Know Before Applying
item.description: Your Marriott Boundless credit limit is assigned by Chase. Understand what is verifiable, how available credit differs, and why your budget comes first.

item.title: Can One JetBlue Trip Offset the Plus Card’s Annual Fee?
item.description: Hypothetical baggage savings of $140 could offset the JetBlue Plus Card’s $99 annual fee. Check eligibility and count only charges you would otherwise pay.

item.title: When a Companion Fare Costs More Than Two Regular Tickets
item.description: A hypothetical $600 companion booking loses to two $275 tickets. Compare the full trip cost before treating a companion fare as savings.

item.title: Before You Count 2% Cash Back, Check Where It Has to Go
item.description: Fidelity’s advertised 2% value depends on where you redeem rewards. Check eligible accounts, the redemption minimum, and automatic deposits.

item.title: Atmos Ascent vs. Summit: Are Your Trips Worth the Extra $300?
item.description: Compare Atmos Ascent and Summit by their companion benefits, annual costs and actual travel usefulness—without assigning imaginary value to perks.

item.title: Travel Portals: Use the Credits and Extra Points, Check the Booking
item.description: Compare Capital One, Chase, Amex and Bilt travel portals, weigh rewards against price, and confirm third-party bookings with the airline or hotel.

item.title: Cents Per Point Explained: What 4x Points Is Actually Worth
item.description: Learn how to calculate cents per point, turn earning multipliers into useful comparisons, and avoid chasing redemption values you would never pay cash for.

item.title: Cash Back or Points? Start With the Work You’ll Actually Do
item.description: Points can deliver outsized value, but transfers take research. Learn what points mean and how to compare their real return with cash back.

item.title: The Boring 2% Card Is the Right First Card
item.description: Start with a flat 2% card: choose cash back or travel rewards, then keep 2% as the floor for ordinary spending.

item.title: Monthly Card Credits Are a Part-Time Job
item.description: Rate card credits by expiration, restrictions, booking steps, and realistic use—not the headline value.

item.title: The Sapphire Reserve’s DoorDash credits are mostly not for takeout
item.description: The Sapphire Reserve’s three monthly DoorDash benefits rise to $35 on October 1, while DashPass remains a separate perk.

item.title: The Organic Spend Test: Would You Buy It Without the Card?
item.description: Use the organic spend test to separate useful card credits from coupons that encourage unnecessary spending.

item.title: Amex Platinum’s $300 Lululemon credit still leaves $595 to justify
item.description: The Amex Platinum now offers $75 in quarterly Lululemon credits, but even full use leaves $595 of its annual fee to justify.

item.title: Your Annual Fee Isn’t the Number That Matters
item.description: Calculate a credit card’s effective annual fee using only credits you would genuinely use, then repeat the math at every renewal.
